prompt.context: A friend has offered to sell you his coffee shop for $100,000.
prompt.question: Should you buy the coffee shop? Is it worth $100,000?

clarifying_info.q: Where is the coffee shop located?
What does the shop sell and at what prices?
clarifying_info.a: Cup of coffee at $4.00, bottled water at $2.00, and pastries at $3.00.

clarifying_info.q: What are the variable costs / margins?
What is the customer base like? Is demand seasonal?
clarifying_info.a: The shop serves mostly locals, not tourists, so demand is consistent throughout the year.
Rent is $500 per month. Wages are $8.00 per hour for 2 employees. The shop is open 12 hours a day, six days a week.

clarifying_info.q: Can I assume consistent profits going forward?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, you can assume the coffee shop will bring in consistent profits.

exhibits.shows: A page from the casebook containing the analysis section with revenue, cost, and valuation calculations.
exhibits.data: Customer flow assumptions, product mix percentages, fixed cost figures, and DCF valuation steps are shown in the analysis section.

framework: Determine annual profitability: estimate revenues, subtract variable costs and fixed costs, apply tax
Revenues: estimate customer volume (market sizing) and revenue per customer (product mix)
Valuation: discount after-tax profits over assumed holding period using WACC to derive NPV; compare to $100,000 asking price
Qualitative check: management experience, competitive landscape, consistency of demand

questions.prompt: Estimate the number of customers per year.
questions.guidance: Use traffic assumptions by hour type. First and last 2 hours are busy (20 customers/hour); remaining 8 hours are slow (10 customers/hour). Saturday is all busy. Apply 50-week year.

math.setup: Weekday customers: 20 customers/hr x 4 busy hours + 10 customers/hr x 8 slow hours = customers per weekday. Saturday: 20 x 12. Weekly total x 5 weekdays + 1 Saturday, then x 50 weeks.
steps: Annual: 1,040 x 50 = 52,000 (casebook rounds to 50,000 for simplicity)

questions.guidance: Apply product mix: 60% order coffee at $4, 30% order pastry at $3, 10% order water at $2.

math.setup: Revenue = customers x (mix% x price) for each product.

questions.guidance: Rent and wages. Note wages cover 2 employees working 12 hours/day, 6 days/week, 50 weeks/year.

math.setup: Rent = monthly rate x 12. Wages = hourly rate x hours/day x days/week x weeks/year x employees.
steps: Wages: $8 x 12 x 6 x 50 = $28,800 (casebook uses $30,000, applying 2 employees: $8 x 2 x 12 x 6 x 50 / note casebook formula shows $8 x 12 x 6 x 50 = $28,800, rounded to $30,000 in the text)

questions.guidance: Apply 50% variable margin to revenue first, then subtract fixed costs to get pre-tax profit. Apply 40% tax rate.

math.setup: Gross profit = Revenue x 50% margin. Operating profit = Gross profit - Fixed costs. After-tax profit = Operating profit x (1 - tax rate).

questions.prompt: Value the coffee shop using DCF and determine whether to buy at $100,000.
questions.guidance: Assume 5-year operating period and 10% WACC. Discount each year's after-tax profit and sum. Compare NPV to $100,000 asking price.

math.setup: Value = sum of PV of $31,500 per year for 5 years discounted at 10%. PV_t = 31,500 / 1.1^(t-1) for t = 1 to 5.
math.answer: NPV ~$131,000 > $100,000 asking price, suggesting the purchase is worthwhile

brainstorming.prompt: What additional factors should be investigated before making the final decision?

categories.name: Demand Sustainability
ideas: Verify that customer base is truly local and not seasonal
Assess risk of major employers or residents leaving the area
Check historical sales data for any trend

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Number and proximity of competing coffee shops
Threat of national chains (Starbucks) entering Vail
Differentiation and loyalty of current customers

categories.name: Management & Operations
ideas: Does the buyer have F&B or management experience?
Can the current staff be retained?

categories.name: Financial Assumptions
ideas: Sensitivity of valuation to changes in WACC or time horizon
Possibility of additional costs: utilities, insurance, maintenance

categories.name: Growth Potential
ideas: Opportunity to expand menu or increase prices

recommendation: Based on the analysis, the coffee shop's NPV of approximately $131,000 exceeds the $100,000 asking price, suggesting it is financially worth purchasing assuming consistent annual profits of ~$31,500 after tax.
The deal generates positive value of ~$31,000 over the asking price, providing a margin of safety.
risks: Demand may not remain consistent if tourism shifts or local demographics change
Competition from national chains could erode customer base
The buyer may lack relevant management experience, increasing operational risk
Key assumptions (product mix, customer count, tax rate) are estimates and actual results may vary
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on historical financials (actual revenue, cost, and profit records)
Assess competitive environment in Vail, Colorado
Evaluate own management capability or cost of hiring a manager
Renegotiate purchase price downward if due diligence reveals weaker performance
